title: Pictograph Builder
context: Grade 4. An adult sees a chart being drawn. What is actually being learnt is that a pictograph is drawn one symbol for each key's worth, that it needs a title and a key to be read at all, and that a column standing up the page is read exactly as a row is. The chapter's one pictograph drawn up the page numbers its side from nought to ten under the heading number of children, but each face stands for two children, so the numbers count faces. This tool reads every column by its symbols and the key, and its side ruler numbers only in the data's own units. The exercise's symbol is printed as a copyright sign, and the tool offers plain pictures only.

writeup.why: Draw a pictograph from a tally chart, one symbol for each key's worth, give it a title and a key, stand it up the page, and read a column by its symbols and the key.
writeup.look: A tally chart at the left, an empty pictograph at the right with a title strip and a key box, a tray of plain picture symbols, and a side ruler.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Pictograph Builder' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the symbols stamped in the row being built, one number in ink that climbs by one for each stamp and shows a half for a half stamp. Beside it are the rows finished against the rows the tally holds. Lifting a stamp takes one off, because the tally gets its marks back. A row's number is never written here, and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The tally chart stands at the left of the working area, 300 by 380 at 64,212. It holds up to six rows, each 56 tall with 6 between, from 220, each with its name in a cell 90 wide and its tally marks in a strip 200 wide. The marks are drawn small, every fifth across the four before it, up to four bundles. The symbol tray sits under it, 300 by 110 at 64,606, holding five plain pictures: a face, a cup, a tree, a kite and a bus. No letter, sign or mark stands in for a picture. The pictograph stands at the right, 660 by 500 at 380,212. Along its top are the title strip, 480 by 44, and the key box, 170 by 44 at 870,212, both outlined blanks until they are filled. Across the page it holds up to six rows, each 56 tall with 8 between, from 268. Each row has its name in a cell 120 wide, then its symbols from 512, each 36 wide with 8 between, up to ten. Its number, with its unit, sits in a tag 80 wide at 956. The key dial card stands at the far right, 100 by 210 at 1048,212, with the turn control under it at 1048,436 and the side ruler control at 1048,510. Each stamp puts one symbol at the next place along its row, one width and one gap on from the last, counted from the row's left edge. At the same moment one key's worth of marks fades from the matching tally row. A half stamp is offered only when exactly half a key's worth is left in that tally row, and it draws the left half of the symbol, last in the row. A stamp with nothing left in its tally row does not land. Every symbol stamped is the same picture at the same size, and a symbol dragged along its row slides back to its place. The pictograph shows as finished only when the title strip and the key box are both filled. The turn control swings the finished rows up into columns, each 64 wide with 24 between, from 464, stacked from a bottom line at 670. Each symbol, 34 tall with 4 between, keeps its place; the column names sit under the line, and each column's number sits above its top symbol. The side ruler, 56 wide at 392, lies blank beside the columns. As each symbol is tapped from the bottom, it writes beside it in amber the key times the symbols counted so far, in the data's own units. It never numbers the symbols themselves. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a number is asked for. For the title and the key's unit, a small letter pad opens over it, with the words the data uses offered as whole keys, children, people, cups, days and books among them. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and every fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in the rows, is green, except where the rows are named by colour. There each row's symbols wear that row's own colour: red, green, blue, yellow or purple. The key's symbol there is plain grey, which stands for one symbol of any colour and is used for nothing else. Amber is what a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, and so are the numbers in a table and the numbers a side ruler writes. Amber too is what half a symbol stands for, what a key leaves over, and a small round counter for one thing counted. A total of every row is reddish purple, and so is a thing a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share. The row a question asks about is marked by a pale sky blue band laid behind its symbols, never over them. So is the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another. Chrome never borrows one of those, and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every table rule, row line, belt, route line, bracket, outlined blank and card edge is near-black, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. Every reading survives with the colour taken away. A fifth mark lies across and not upright, and a half symbol is the left half of the whole. A row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it. No amount is ever drawn as a length of colour: an amount on this stage is symbols, marks, counters or a written number. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. No pictograph on this stage is drawn with its side numbered in symbols. A side is left bare, or the side ruler numbers it in the data's own units, so a number the stage writes beside a column counts the data and not the pictures.
writeup.finish: The card shows the pictograph the child drew from the tally, with its title and its key, standing up the page, and the side ruler numbered in children beside one column.

phases.win: the last marks fade from the tally as the last symbol lands, and the row's count matches
phases.does: stamps symbols into the row, each taking one key's worth of marks from the tally, until the tally row is used up
phases.goal: one symbol is drawn for each key's worth, so the count shared into the key gives the number of symbols
phases.says: Each symbol stands for this many. How many symbols use up the tally?
phases.check: The key is one face for five people. How many faces show thirty people?
phases.feels: each stamp takes its handful of marks from the tally, and the row is done when the tally is
phases.hands: Before the tool is opened, tally the class's favourite fruits on the board. Then build the pictograph on the wall with one sticky note for every two children, crossing two marks off the tally for each note. Ask how many notes the mango row needs before anyone sticks one up. The count is shared into twos, not counted one by one, and a row with one child left over would need half a note.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many does one symbol stand for? Second rung, the phase's: how many of those make the count? Third rung: the tally row is cut to six marks with a key of two, and the child stamps until it is used up. The number keys stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: one picture for one child is how pictures have always counted, and the key is easy to forget while drawing.
wrong.move: tries to stamp one face for each child, fourteen faces for fourteen children.
wrong.screen: each stamp fades two marks from the tally, and after seven stamps the tally row is used up. The eighth stamp does not land, and the row stands at seven faces. Lifting a face gives its two marks back to the tally.

wrong.why: the bundles are what the eye sees in a tally, and each looks like one thing to draw.
wrong.move: stamps one face for each bundle of five in the tally, two faces for fourteen.
wrong.screen: the first stamp fades two marks out of the first bundle, not the whole bundle, and the bundle is seen split. The row goes on to seven faces as the tally fades two marks at a time.

wrong.why: the favourite row feels as though it ought to look the biggest.
wrong.move: wants the favourite row's pictures drawn bigger or further apart, so it reaches past a row with more symbols.
wrong.screen: every stamp lands the same picture at the same size, at the next place along from the row's left edge. A symbol dragged further along slides back, and the row stands at its true length, shorter than the row with more symbols.

phases.screen: a tally chart at the left, an empty pictograph row at the right, and the key dial set
phases.soWhat: Draw one symbol for each key's worth. The symbols times the key give back the count.

phases.win: the title and the key fill in, and every row's number appears at its end
phases.does: writes a title that says what the data is about and fills the key box
phases.goal: every pictograph needs a title that says what the data is about and a key that says what one symbol stands for
phases.says: Could anyone read this yet? What is missing?
phases.check: Away from the screen: draw three rows of stars for your class's pets. Give it a title and a key.
phases.feels: the chart can be read only once it says what it counts and what each picture is worth
phases.hands: Hold up a chart with no title and no key, and ask what it shows and how many each row is. Let the class find that nobody can say. The vocabulary box lists title and never defines it, and leaves out key altogether, so say both: the title is the heading that says what a pictograph shows, and the key says what one symbol stands for. The third exercise prints its symbol as a sign, not a picture. Draw a plain picture instead, and call its categories kinds of television show.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does one picture stand for? Second rung, the phase's: could someone else read this chart? Third rung: the chart is cut to one row, and the child fills its key box. The letter pad stays open.

wrong.why: the child drew the chart and knows the key, so it does not feel missing.
wrong.move: leaves the key off because the pictures are easy to count, so a reader takes each picture as one flower.
wrong.screen: the pictograph will not show as finished, and the key box stays an outlined blank. Each row's tag stays empty, and the running count shows symbols only. The child's rows stay as drawn.

wrong.why: a title looks like a name for the picture, and the picture is a pictograph.
wrong.move: writes a title that names the chart but not the data, such as My Pictograph.
wrong.screen: the title strip keeps the child's words. A question card beside it asks what was counted, and the strip is offered back with the child's words still in it.

wrong.why: the number is the part used for reading, so it seems to be the whole key.
wrong.move: writes the key as one flower for five, without saying five of what.
wrong.screen: the key box keeps the number, and its unit stays an outlined blank. Each row's tag writes its number with the same blank after it.

phases.screen: a finished set of rows with the title strip and the key box still outlined blanks
phases.soWhat: Every pictograph needs a title that says what the data is about and a key that says what one symbol stands for.

phases.win: the rows swing up into columns, every symbol keeps its place, and the column's number matches its row's
phases.does: stands it up the page, then reads one column by counting its symbols and using the key
phases.goal: a pictograph drawn up the page is read the same way, by counting symbols and using the key
phases.says: Now it stands up. Is it read any differently?
phases.check: A column holds five faces, one face for four children. How many children does it show?
phases.feels: the rows swing up, every symbol keeps its place, and a column is read just as its row was
phases.hands: Stand the class's fruit pictograph up the wall, one column for each fruit, sticking the notes on from the bottom. Ask whether it is read any differently. The chapter says pictographs are usually drawn across the page and can be drawn up it. Its one upward pictograph is the zoo animals, eight faces for the tiger at two children each.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many symbols are in the column? Second rung, the phase's: what does one symbol stand for? Third rung: the pictograph is cut to one column of three symbols, and the child reads it from the bottom. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: a column standing up looks like a new kind of chart, and its height looks like the answer.
wrong.move: counts the column's symbols and gives six as the children who come by bicycle, forgetting the key once it stands up.
wrong.screen: the column's symbols light from the bottom one at a time into the running count, six. The key's three is taken under each, and eighteen lands above the column. The child's six stays in the slot.

wrong.why: writing starts at the top of a page, and the title is at the top.
wrong.move: on a pictograph drawn by hand, hangs each column's symbols from the top, so a short column starts high and looks tall.
wrong.screen: the child's drawing stays on its card beside the board. The turned pictograph stacks every column from the bottom line, so a short column is short at the foot, and the columns' numbers are the same as before.

phases.screen: the finished pictograph across the page with the turn control waiting
phases.soWhat: A pictograph drawn up the page is read the same way: count the symbols and use the key.

phases.win: the side ruler reads in children up to the top face, and the answer matches the column
phases.does: counts the faces, uses the key, and numbers the side ruler in children as each face is tapped
phases.goal: a column's data is its symbols times the key, whatever numbers stand beside it
phases.says: Those numbers count faces. How many children does the column show?
phases.check: Each face stands for three children. What numbers go beside the first four faces?
phases.feels: the numbers climb up the side by the key's worth, and the top one is the column's number
phases.hands: Show the chapter's upward pictograph of zoo animals. Its side is numbered from nought to ten in ones at the grid lines, under a heading that names children. Each face fills one grid square and stands for two children, so those numbers count faces: the tiger's column reaches eight where sixteen children chose it. Read every column by counting its faces and using the key. If the class numbers a side, number it in children, two, four, six, or leave it bare.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what do the numbers on the side count? Second rung, the phase's: what does one face stand for? Third rung: the column is cut to three faces, and the child numbers the side ruler in children. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: a number beside a column usually says how much the column is, and the heading says children.
wrong.move: reads seven off the numbered side as the children, when those numbers count faces.
wrong.screen: the side ruler is laid blank beside the column. As each face is tapped from the bottom it writes two, four, six in amber, and it reaches fourteen at the top face. The child's seven stays beside the old side's seven.

wrong.why: the chapter's own upward pictograph does exactly that, so it looks like the right way.
wrong.move: numbers the side of their own upward pictograph one per face, under the heading number of children.
wrong.screen: the side ruler is laid beside the child's side and numbers itself in children as each face is tapped, two, four, six, up to the key times the faces. The child's numbers stand beside it, and the heading is set against both.

phases.screen: one column of faces with the key above it, a question card describing a side numbered one per face, and the side ruler blank
phases.soWhat: A column's data is its symbols times the key, whatever numbers stand beside it.

writeup.delight: The first phase, when the last symbol of a row lands and its tally row is used up. The faded marks drift across the stage and settle inside the symbols, a key's worth in each whole symbol and half that in a half. Every symbol is seen holding its own marks. A tap on any symbol afterwards makes its marks glow inside it for a moment. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked either way, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the tally chart stands at the left with the key dial already set. One empty row waits on the pictograph at the right, with the symbol tray open. On the second the rows stand finished, with the title strip and the key box still outlined blanks. On the third the finished pictograph stands across the page with the turn control waiting. On the fourth one column of faces stands up the page with the key above it, and the side ruler lies blank beside it. A question card in the slot describes a side numbered one per face. The running count at the top left holds the symbols stamped in the row being built, with the rows finished beside it. The answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the stamp, or the empty key box, or the turn control, or the column's bottom face, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks its question. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any tally chart of up to six rows, any plain picture symbol and any key that fits, across the page or up it, with the side ruler open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on symbols from a tally, the title and the key, pictographs drawn up the page, and numbers beside a column.
voiceLines: A tally on one side and an empty pictograph on the other. Set the key first.
Each symbol stands for this many. How many symbols use up the tally?
Could anyone read this yet? What is missing?
Now it stands up. Is it read any differently?
Those numbers count faces. How many children does the column show?
Another tally. How much does one symbol take from it?
Free play. Any tally, any plain picture, and any key that fits.
Lift the last symbol off, and watch how many marks it gives back.
A pictograph drawn from its tally, given a title and a key, and read standing up.

observations.why: Each symbol stood for one key's worth, so it took that many marks.
observations.soWhat: One symbol is drawn for each key's worth: the count shared into the key gives the number of symbols.
observations.observe: Each stamp faded two marks from the tally, and the row was finished when the tally row was used up.

observations.why: Without the key nobody can turn a symbol into a number, and without the title nobody knows what was counted.
observations.soWhat: Every pictograph needs a title that says what the data is about and a key that says what one symbol stands for.
observations.observe: The pictograph would not show as finished until its title and its key were both filled.

observations.why: Turning moves the symbols, and it does not change how many there are or what each one stands for.
observations.soWhat: A pictograph drawn up the page is read the same way: count the symbols and use the key.
observations.observe: The rows swung up into columns, and every column's number matched its row's.

observations.why: It writes the key times the symbols counted, which is the data and not the count of symbols.
observations.soWhat: Numbers beside a column count whatever they were written for, and the column's data is its symbols times the key.
observations.observe: The side ruler wrote two, four, six up the column, and its top number matched the column's number.

serves.exercise: preparing a tally chart and a pictograph of the favourite kinds of television show of a group of people

source_tool.description: A tally chart stands at the left of the stage and an empty pictograph at the right, with a tray of plain picture symbols, faces, cups, trees, kites and buses, and a key card with a value dial. The child sets the key, then stamps symbols into a row one at a time; each stamp takes one key's worth of marks from the matching tally row, the marks fading from the tally as they are used, so the row is finished when the tally is used up, and a half symbol is offered only when exactly half a key's worth is left. A title strip and a key box sit on the pictograph as outlined blanks, and the pictograph will not show as finished until both are filled. A turn control stands the finished pictograph up the page, the rows becoming columns stacked from the bottom, each symbol keeping its place. A side ruler can be laid beside the columns and numbers itself only in the data's own units, two, four, six for a key of two, as the child taps each symbol; it never numbers the symbols themselves. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts symbols, and each column's number is written above it with its unit, so the two are never confused.
source_tool.art_direction: Picture stamps beside a tally chart / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a desk with a drawn class and a heap of answer slips, a ruled table, a tally board with a belt of answer cards, pictograph boards with a title strip and a key card, symbols that fold down their middle, a small route map, a tray of picture stamps, and a key dial.
Every pictograph carries a title strip at its top and a key card beside it from the first frame. A title or key still to be filled is an outlined blank, never a space left out.

Every symbol in one pictograph is one plain picture drawn at one size, evenly spaced from the same edge in every row or column, so a row's length is its count of symbols. A face, a kite, a cup, a tree or a bus; no letter, sign or mark ever stands in for a picture.

When the rows of a pictograph name colours, each row's symbols, whole or half, are drawn in that row's colour, and the key's symbol in plain grey. Otherwise every symbol in one pictograph, the key's included, is drawn in one colour.

A half symbol is the left half of the whole symbol, cut down its middle, as the chapter's own keys show it. It always comes last in its row. Halves are the only part of a symbol ever drawn, and only on a key that halves into whole things.
A tally mark is one short upright line. Every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, corner to corner, and the next mark starts a new bundle after a small gap.
A pictograph drawn up the page stacks its symbols from the bottom. Its side is left unnumbered, or numbered only in the data's own units, the key times the symbols counted, and never in symbols.

The count of symbols and the number they stand for are never written in the same place: symbols are counted at the top left of the canvas, and a row's number is written at the end of its row with its unit.
The sum of every row is written under the board, labelled as the total for all the rows, and never beside a single row.
A row, a symbol or a mark is told apart by its name or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a tally mark, a symbol, a number, a band or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and the fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that counts in fives cannot afford a bundle whose closing mark has to be hunted for. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in every row, is green, except where the rows are told apart by colour: there every symbol in a row is that row's own colour, red, green, blue, yellow or purple, and the key's symbol is plain grey, a grey used for nothing else, because it stands for a symbol of any colour. What a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, the number written beyond a row's end, the numbers in a table, the numbers a side ruler writes in the data's own units, what half a symbol stands for, and what a key leaves over, is amber. A total of every row, and a thing that a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share, are reddish purple. The row a question asks about, and the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another, are marked by a pale sky blue band behind the symbols or marks. Every table rule, row line, belt, bracket, outlined blank and card border is near-black chrome, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. All of that holds in greyscale, because a fifth mark lies across and not upright, a half symbol is the left half of the whole, a row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Lift the last symbol off, and watch how many marks it gives back.
voice.onNext: Another tally. How much does one symbol take from it?
voice.opening: A tally on one side and an empty pictograph on the other. Set the key first.
voice.onFinish: A pictograph drawn from its tally, given a title and a key, and read standing up.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any tally, any plain picture, and any key that fits.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After a tally of favourite fruits has been built up the classroom wall with one sticky note for every two children, and before the printed exercise is drawn. The tool is what takes one key's worth from the tally for every symbol stamped, refuses to finish a pictograph without its title and key, and numbers a side only in the data's own units.

answer_key.rule: A pictograph is drawn by choosing a symbol and a key, then drawing one symbol for each key's worth in every row: the count shared into the key's worth gives the number of symbols, and a half symbol stands for half a key's worth left over. Every pictograph needs a title, which says what the data is about, and a key, which says what one symbol stands for. A pictograph can run across the page or up it, and a column is read exactly as a row is, by counting its symbols and using the key. Numbers written beside a column count whatever they were written for; when they count symbols, the column's data is still its symbols times the key.
answer_key.wrong: The stamps are lifted off one at a time and each gives its key's worth back to the tally, so the child sees how many marks each symbol used, and the side ruler renumbers the column in the data's own units as each symbol is tapped. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Each face stands for 2 children, so find how many twos make 14.
14 shared into twos is 7, because 7 x 2 = 14.
Draw 7 faces in the swimming row.
items.question: A tally chart shows 14 children chose swimming, and the key is one face for 2 children. How many faces go in the swimming row?
items.checkpoint: Draw one symbol for each key's worth; the symbols times the key give back the count.
items.misconception: Drawing one face for each child, 14 faces, as though each face stood for one child.

steps: The title is the heading that says what the pictograph shows: here, the flowers in bloom today.
The key says what one symbol stands for: one flower picture for 5 flowers.
Without the key the pictures cannot be turned into numbers, and without the title nobody knows what was counted.
items.answer: A title such as Flowers in Bloom Today, and the key one flower picture for 5 flowers
items.question: A pictograph has rows of flower pictures for four gardens, but no title and no key. Each picture stands for 5 flowers, and the chart counts the flowers in bloom today. What title and key should it carry, and why?
items.checkpoint: Every pictograph needs a title and a key.
items.misconception: Leaving the key off because the pictures are easy to count, so a reader takes each picture as one flower.

steps: Count the symbols in the column from the bottom: there are 6.
This is exactly how a row is read. Only the direction has changed.
items.question: A pictograph drawn up the page has a column of 6 bicycle pictures for Class 4A, and the key is one bicycle for 3 children. How many children in Class 4A come by bicycle?
items.checkpoint: A pictograph that stands up is read like one across: count the symbols and use the key.
items.misconception: Treating the column as a new kind of chart and reading how high it reaches, instead of counting its symbols and using the key.

steps: The numbers on that side count faces, not children.
Count the faces, 7, and use the key: 7 x 2 = 14.
Numbered in children, the side would read 2, 4, 6 and so on up to 14.
items.question: An upward pictograph has a column of 7 faces, each for 2 children. A chart numbers the side beside it one to seven, one number for each face. How many children does the column show?
items.checkpoint: A column is read by counting its symbols and using the key.
items.misconception: Reading 7 off the numbered side as the number of children, when those numbers count faces.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: The key is one star for 2 children. How many stars show 22 children?
The key is one book picture for 5 books. How many book pictures show 35 books?
A pictograph shows rows of cup pictures but has no key, and a friend reads each row as that many cups. What should the pictograph have carried?
items.final_answer: A key saying what one cup picture stands for, and a title saying what the data is about

items.question: A class drew a pictograph of rainy days in four months with one cloud for 2 days, but left off the key. June holds 6 clouds, and a reader says June had 6 rainy days. How many rainy days did June have?
items.final_answer: 12, because each cloud stands for 2 days. The missing key misled the reader

items.question: An upward pictograph has columns of 4, 7 and 5 cup pictures, and one cup stands for 10 cups of tea. How many cups does each column show?
The same data is drawn once across the page and once up it. The mango row of the one across holds 9 symbols. How many symbols does the mango column of the upward one hold?
items.final_answer: 9. Only the direction changes, so every row keeps its symbols

items.question: A column holds 9 faces, each for 5 people. Its side is numbered one to nine, one number per face, under the heading Number of people. How many people does the column show?
items.final_answer: 45. The side's numbers count faces, so the heading does not match them: 9 x 5 = 45 people

items.question: You number the side of an upward pictograph in children, with one face for 4 children. What numbers go beside the first, second, third and fourth faces?

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds plain picture symbols: faces, cups, trees, kites and buses
sets what one symbol stands for before any symbol is stamped
puts one symbol in a row and takes one key's worth from its tally
offered only when exactly half a key's worth is left in a tally row
an outlined blank the pictograph cannot be finished without
an outlined blank for the key, also needed to finish
stands the pictograph up the page, rows becoming columns from the bottom
numbers a column's side in the data's own units as each symbol is tapped

teaching_notes: Tally the class's favourite fruits before the tool is opened, and build the pictograph up the wall with one sticky note for every two children. Ask how many children one column shows, and why the number of notes is not the answer on its own. The chapter's one pictograph drawn up the page numbers its side from nought to ten in ones under the heading number of children, but each face stands for two children, so the numbers count faces, and the tiger's column reaches eight where sixteen children chose it. Read every column by counting its symbols and using the key. If the class numbers a side, number it in the data's own units, two, four, six, or leave it unnumbered. The exercise's symbol is printed as a copyright sign; draw a plain picture instead, a small face or a television. The same exercise calls its categories a programme, a channel and kinds of show; call them kinds of television show. Every count in that exercise is even and its key is two, so no half symbol is needed there.
generation_prompt: Build a pictograph drawing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A tally chart of up to six rows stands at the left of the working area and an empty pictograph at the right, with a tray of plain picture symbols, faces, cups, trees, kites and buses, and a key card with a value dial above it. Stamping a symbol into a row fades one key's worth of tally marks from the matching tally row; a half stamp is offered only when exactly half a key's worth is left, and draws the left half of the symbol at the row's end. A title strip and a key box sit on the pictograph as outlined blanks, and the finished state is refused until both are filled. A turn control rotates the pictograph so its rows become columns stacked from the bottom, every symbol keeping its place and size. A side ruler beside the columns stays blank until the child taps a symbol, then writes beside each symbol, in the data's own units, the key times the symbols counted so far; it never numbers symbols. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts symbols, and each column's number is written above it with its unit. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Set the key first. Stamp one symbol for each key's worth. Give the pictograph a title and a key. Stand it up the page. Count the symbols in a column. Then use the key.
